title: Designing your life and your freedom number
audience: Any home-service operator, including solo operators, starting or growing a business.
learningOutcomes: Describe your core values and the working life you want
Calculate the income your business must replace to cover your lifestyle
Write a dated goal for time you want back

instruction.heading: Why start with your life, not the business
instruction.body: A business is a tool for the life you want. Before you quote a job, decide what you want less of (for example, financial worry), what you want more of (for example, time with family), and what a normal week should look like. These answers set the limits for how much work you take and what you charge.

instruction.heading: Your freedom number
instruction.body: Work out your lifestyle cost: rent or mortgage, bills, insurance, vehicle, tax, savings and personal spending. That total is the income your business must reach before you can say it has replaced your job. A separate dream number can be set later, once the first one is reached.

instruction.heading: Time you want back
instruction.body: Write down how many hours per week you want to claim back and what they are for. Use this when you decide how many jobs per week you can safely take, and how much travel time each job adds.

instruction.heading: Writing it down
instruction.body: Keep the answers in one document. Revisit them every three months. The goalposts can move; the point is to have a clear reason for the work.

procedure: List five values in order of importance.
Write three things you want less of and three you want more of.
Draft a typical week, hour by hour.
Calculate your freedom number from your real monthly costs.
Set a date by which you want to reach that number and the hours you want back.

workedExamples.situation: A licensed handyman earns $X a week but wants Friday afternoons free. The freedom number shows he needs one more regular client per month, not four.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What job volume and price does that require?
workedExamples.reasoning: The number of jobs and the price per job both follow from the freedom number and the hours available. Working backwards avoids overbooking.

commonErrors.error: Writing values that sound good but do not affect decisions
commonErrors.prevention: Test each value against one real decision you face this month.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out tax and insurance from the freedom number
commonErrors.prevention: Include every cost, then add a margin for quiet months.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business guidance only. This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority. Check state or territory rules before acting.

qualityStandard: Offer and pricing decisions are written down and checked against cost and time.
documentationEvidence: Written offer or plan, evidence collected, and the decision made.
summary: Your freedom number is the first business target.
Time you want back limits how much work you can accept.
Revisit the answers every three months.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the freedom number?
options: The income needed to cover your full lifestyle costs
The total turnover of the business
The price of your most popular service, multiplied by twelve
The number of hours you can work each week

knowledgeChecks.question: Why include tax and insurance in the freedom number?
options: Because they are optional for trades businesses
Because they are part of the real cost of living
Because they reduce the business price

knowledgeChecks.question: When should the freedom number be revisited?
options: Only once, at the start and never again
Only when a customer complains, rarely
Every three months, or when costs change
Only at the year-end review, at most

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the lesson say goes into the lifestyle cost?
options: Only the price of the most popular service
Only the hours worked each week
Rent or mortgage, bills, insurance, vehicle, tax, savings and personal spending

sourceReferences: Solopreneur Start-Up Guide, Step 1 (Tom Scourfield; distribution rights held by the user). Adapted for home-service operators; sales pitch at the end of the guide omitted.
